title: How sample size changes the margin of error
subtitle: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error  · 3 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **3 of the official questions in Inference from sample statistics and margin of error  are this one** — 0 Easy, 1 Medium, 2 Hard.
It is top-heavy: most versions are Hard, so it only earns study time once your target actually requires that tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- You're comparing two samples from the same population with MOEs computed the same way, or a researcher is choosing between a smaller and a larger sample, or a sample size gets multiplied.
- The question asks why one MOE is bigger, what happens to the MOE, or what range the new MOE falls in.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Larger sample means smaller MOE, and smaller sample means larger MOE.
- The sample's percent or estimate is NOT the reason.
- 2) If the size is multiplied by k, the MOE is divided by √k.
- Doubling the size cuts the MOE to about 0.71 of its original, so it is smaller but NOT halved.

sections.heading: Where Desmos fits
body: Type originalMOE/sqrt(2) (or /sqrt(k)) to place the new MOE in the correct range.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You say the larger sample has the larger MOE.
You credit the difference to the sample's higher percent in favor.
Or, on the scaling version, you assume doubling the sample halves the MOE.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
You say the larger sample has the larger MOE.
You credit the difference to the sample's higher percent in favor.
